title: Rich vs Poor: Dinner Before the French Revolution
alternate_titles: Two Dinners in Paris, 1783. Which Table Is Yours?
What Did Rich and Poor Parisians Eat Before the Revolution?
period: Paris, 1783; two explicitly composite households illustrate unequal meals using contemporary observations and an earlier Paris cookbook still suitable as a period recipe source. Do not claim a recorded dinner on a particular day. Late Ancien Régime city: narrow irregular streets, modest stone/plaster shopfronts and wooden shutters; market stalls before Baltard's nineteenth-century halls. Locals in restrained eighteenth-century shirts, waistcoats, knee breeches, coats, skirts and practical caps/aprons. Affluent household is prosperous urban, not the royal court at Versailles. Kitchens use masonry hearths, spit and copper/iron/earthenware vessels; no gas range. Modest room has one small hearth, plain bowl and substantial round loaf, not modern baguette. Summer/early autumn produce and light; no snow. Visitor composited from unchanged normal outfit as neutral guide.
avoid: Eiffel Tower, Haussmann boulevards, Baltard iron market halls, modern baguettes or croissants, chef toques, stainless-steel kitchen islands, gas/electric cookers, identical powdered wigs on everybody, royal throne at a Paris household dinner, invented Marie Antoinette cake quote, blood or carcass gore, every poor person starving or meatless, all rich leftovers thrown away, fake text on menus, modern restaurant plating, ethnic caricatures from Mercier's polemic

modest.frame: illustrative composite, not a named household
modest.design: Small clean but worn plaster room with left hearth, narrow window, plain table and two stools. Two adults in muted working clothes; one round brownish bread loaf, simple ceramic bowls and a small portion of sausage only when specified. No grotesque filth or starvation anatomy.

rich.frame: illustrative composite, not a recorded banquet
rich.design: Comfortable panelled dining room with tall window, modest gilt mirror and white-clothed table, a few faience/porcelain dishes and silver serving utensils. Two adult diners and one servant maximum. Roast poultry, cabbage garnish and small sauce bowl; abundance without a mountainous fantasy feast.

market.design: Open pre-nineteenth-century food market with stone/plaster edges, wooden tables and hand baskets. Seasonal fruit, vegetables, bread and covered meat baskets in separate stalls. No iron/glass pavilion, readable price signs or repeated fountain.

shop.design: Low stone/plaster shopfront with open wooden counter, two golden pies and one prepared poultry dish displayed under shade, inner masonry oven visible. No glass bakery cabinet or neon branding.

bread.design: Round or oval substantial loaf with imperfect crust on plain wood; no long narrow modern baguette or fake baker stamp.

sausage.design: One small cooked sausage portion on plain dish beside cut bread, not a measured facsimile of Mercier's three-sol purchase. No exact size or nutrient claim.

kitchen.design: Masonry hearth and spit at left, stable wooden worktable front, hanging restrained copper pans and iron pot; one adult cook in simple cap and apron, one assistant only if requested. Cabbage, mushroom, garlic and small ham piece kept separate until recipe stage.

cabbage.scope: Recipe illustration from Menon,Les Soupers de la Cour1755,volIII p24; demonstrated in1783scenario
cabbage.frame: period recipe demonstration, not a recorded household meal
cabbage.design: One quartered green cabbage on wood worktop, plain pot, earthen bowl and cloth. Ingredient geometry stays consistent through cooking stages. No cabbage assumed to identify poverty or wealth on its own.

sauce.design: Small plain pan at left of wood worktop, separate mushrooms, ham slice, garlic clove with one spice clove, bowl of brown stock/coulis, coarse pepper; simple sieve and receiving bowl. No modern measuring jug.

oven.scope: Paris,1783; commercial oven described by Mercier
oven.design: Masonry bakery oven with arched mouth and plain wooden peel, two distinguishable household earthenware dishes on adjacent bench, one baker in simple linen cap. Show limited illustrative load, not exact claimed fifty meals.

service.scope: Paris,1783; composite wealthy household service space
service.design: Plain side table beyond wealthy dining-room doorway, modest serving plates with remaining roast poultry and bread. Ordinary servant may sit or serve without appearing wealthy or clownish; no assumption all leftovers went to this person.

pastry.design: Same kitchen worktable but separate close-up family: chopped cooked poultry, plain filling bowl, thin pastry and crescent-shaped turnovers, no modern puff-pastry branding.

editorial.design: Channel parchment, sparse ingredient/function diagrams and short source qualifications. No invented historical facsimile.

oven_customer_home.scope: Paris,1783; a separate composite household using a commercial oven
oven_customer_home.design: Different small room from first poor household: pale olive plaster, right-side hearth and left square window, simple board table with covered earthenware meat dish. This family can afford a roast but economizes on cooking fuel. Distinct floor plan, clothes and people; do not reuse first household as if its menu has changed.

sources.read: 2026-10-09: title/imprint, p24 cabbage recipe, pp26–28 rissoles and pp29–33 roast preparation/seasonal poultry.

claims.claim: Two imagined households and the Visitor's choice are composite framing for Paris1783, not a recovered day's menu or a claim that all rich/poor people ate alike.
claims.limit: No invented names, household accounts, exact daily budget or universal meal.

claims.claim: Mercier describes abundant food at Les Halles and prominent pastry, charcuterie and roast-food displays in Paris.
claims.limit: Availability in shops does not establish affordability for all; do not reproduce his precise counts or every-day guarantees.

claims.claim: Mercier calls bread a principal food of the urban poor.
claims.locator: Chapter631 paragraph beginning Le pain qu'on mange à Paris.
claims.limit: Not their sole food, not a quantified calorie percentage; no modern nutrition equivalence.

claims.claim: Mercier gives an example of a poor household whose small sausage purchase supplies its limited good fare, and argues small purchases can be costly.
claims.locator: Chapter67 paragraph Plus les classes sont indigentes.
claims.limit: One author's example, not a universal diet or measured representative family; no assertion the portion was all calories for a whole day.

claims.claim: His account also names soup and boiled beef, evening beef dishes and Sunday mutton among ordinary Parisian meals.
claims.limit: Do not turn his broad rhetorical population estimate into data or suggest these meals were within every destitute person's reach.

claims.claim: The relevant comparison includes quantity, choice, preparation and access, not a rule that poor people ate no meat or that cabbage meant poverty.
claims.locator: Ordinary-meal and sausage passages; Menon cabbage recipe.
claims.limit: Synthesis of cited examples, not a claim of identical diets or an affordability index.

claims.claim: Menon's1755cookbook lists roast poultry by season and explains spit preparation; poultry also appears in Mercier's roast-shop descriptions.
claims.limit: Supports an illustrative affluent poultry dish, not a specific1783banquet menu or universal luxury item.

claims.claim: Menon's cabbage recipe blanches, cools and squeezes the cabbage, then braises it and serves it around meat.
claims.limit: Descriptive history, not modern recipe/safety advice; no unsourced exact cooking times.

claims.claim: Its sauce uses ham,mushrooms,garlic with a clove,broth/coulis; it is reduced,strained and finished with pepper.
claims.limit: Do not replace cabbage sauce with neighbouring cauliflower's butter recipe. No invented cream in this particular sauce.

claims.claim: This recipe demonstrates that an ordinary vegetable can involve multiple ingredients,stages,fuel and skilled work; the finished plate hides some preparation.
claims.limit: No measured labour hours,cost or assumption every wealthy household used this recipe.

claims.claim: Mercier describes small households with limited hearths sending meat to pastry-shop ovens, partly to save wood; they pay for cooking.
claims.limit: Modest households able to buy meat, not necessarily the poorest. No universal home-oven absence or exact charge schedule.

claims.claim: Mercier says some wealthy-household servants ate better than modest bourgeois because lavish tables left food; this is his social observation.
claims.locator: Chapter67 un laquais; chapter383 on service and food.
claims.limit: Explicitly attributed, not every servant, not proof servants had more power or better lives than employers.

claims.claim: Menon gives a rissoles recipe starting with leftover roast poultry, turning it into filling enclosed in thin pastry and fried as crescents.
claims.locator: VolumeIII p26,Rissoles à la Béchamel; p27game alternative separately.
claims.limit: Use poultry recipe only; do not claim all leftovers followed this route or identify it as a modern croquette.

claims.claim: Mercier uses sharp social criticism and staged dialogue mocking wealthy diners' demands for novelty; this differs from a prescriptive cookbook. Neither supplies a whole society's actual menu or a single cause of revolution.
claims.limit: No cake quotation, famine spectacle or claim dinner alone caused1789.

research: Set Paris1783, using a composite modest household and a composite affluent urban household. Avoid substituting Versailles for every prosperous city house. Main twist: a cabbage can be an elaborate meat-garnish recipe, and access to fuel/cooks/shop ovens changes what reaches a plate. Mercier is a vivid contemporary critic, not a neutral dataset. His own ordinary-meal account (soup,boiled beef,Sunday mutton) refutes a blanket meatless-poor narrative. His sausage anecdote supports a small purchase, not an invented complete daily ration. Read his surrounding social polemic to avoid adopting stereotypes or fantastical statistical certainty. Menon's1755Paris cookbook independently supports exact preparation sequences and planned reuse of roast poultry, challenging the idea that all rich leftovers were waste. It is a prescription, so the narrator explicitly chooses a period recipe for the reconstruction. No unverified causal claim linking one menu directly to revolution. Food and labour remain the story; methodological qualifications are concise. No modern dollar conversions or precise household food budget. Bibliographic date verified by Wellcome. Cairn's2004butcher-hygiene study was inaccessible except snippets and is not used.
description:
Two tables in Paris,1783: a small meal stretched carefully, and a dinner with more choice, ingredients and labour behind it.

But the contrast is stranger than 'meat versus no meat.' We follow food through the market, a household kitchen, a shared oven and the servants' side of the table—and find an unexpectedly elaborate cabbage along the way. The households are illustrated composites; the observations and recipes come from period sources.
pinned_comment: What surprised you most: the cabbage sauce, paying to use a shop's oven, or who might eat the leftovers?

chapters.title: Two tables, one city
scenes: Two dinners are being prepared in Paris. At one table, the problem is choosing. At the other, it is making enough.
Modest room with round loaf and empty ceramic bowl on table, two adults calmly preparing, no starvation anatomy.
Our rich household can request another dish. The modest household must stretch a small purchase.
Comfortable dining room with white cloth and a few empty serving dishes; servant sets table, no excessive feast.
You arrive in seventeen eighty-three, before the Revolution. Which table would you choose, and what separates them?
Modest table in left foreground, Visitor right thoughtful; no comparison portal or modern menu.
The obvious answer is more food. But watch the cabbage, the oven and the platter after it leaves the dining room.
One fresh cabbage quarter on worktop, plain pot behind; no recipe words painted.
This will be more interesting than rich people eating meat while everybody else chews a crust.
Small sausage portion beside substantial bread slice on modest plain dish.
Our households are composites, based on contemporary observations and a cookbook rather than recovered invitations.
Two simple household silhouettes and one book icon, no invented named family documents.
One guide is the writer Louis-Sébastien Mercier. He had a sharp eye, and equally sharp opinions about the people around him.
Morning market with ordinary adult shoppers and varied goods; no invented portrait of author.
His sharp opinions need care. Alongside them, the cookbook supplies instructions for actual preparations.
Plain closed book on kitchen table, source title composed locally, no fake manuscript lettering.
First, follow the ingredients. Both tables depend on a city where food is visible, tempting, and unevenly within reach.
Roast-food shop display with one poultry dish, two pies and plain counter; no painted lettering.
The Visitor discovers a problem with looking at dinner. Looking is considerably cheaper than buying.
Food display left, Visitor close-up right; no modern wallet or price sign.

chapters.title: The market does not belong equally to everyone
scenes: Mercier describes abundance at Les Halles: fruit, flowers and food. This city has an appetite.
Daylight wooden market stalls with restrained seasonal produce and flowers, no iron halls.
Les Halles • before the nineteenth-century pavilions
The pastry and roast-food shops are equally persuasive. He lists poultry, hams, pies and sugared cakes displayed where people can see them.
One modest ham, poultry dish, two pies and small cakes at counter; avoid food pyramid.
The food itself supplies the advertisement. Our Visitor understands the sales pitch immediately.
Golden pie and cooked poultry prominent left, no readable shop banner.
The city can offer plenty of choice. That does not put the same choices inside every customer's basket.
Two adults at separate stalls, one large market basket and one small hand basket; no class caricatures.
Mercier watches buyers for wealthy households taking what they want, while smaller households compete for what their money can cover.
Household buyer at produce stall left; modest shopper waits nearby, no violence or stolen food.
He blames luxury fiercely. That is social criticism, not a complete explanation of every food price.
Market buyers continue ordinary transactions; Visitor observes rather than accuses.
A more useful detail is his attention to small purchases. Having less money can mean buying a fragment rather than a convenient larger quantity.
Small sausage portion beside a larger uncut piece on vendor board; no precise weight or price.
His poor household's little sausage is a limited treat, rather than an exercise in choosing an impressive dinner.
One small sausage portion wrapped in plain cloth, no paper receipt.
Mercier’s poor-household example • not a universal menu
For our composite meal, we pair the small purchase with bread. The portion is illustrative, not a recovered family account.
Plain loaf, small sausage portion and simple bowl placed on modest table; no exact daily-ration chart.
At the other end of the comparison, a buyer can think about the next dish, the sauce and how the table will look.
Servant arranges several modest dishes on white cloth, empty poultry platter at centre.
Same market, different choices. One basket carries possibilities; the other needs to make a small purchase serve.
Two clearly different-sized baskets on stall, no labels implying actual measured budgets.
Now take the smaller basket home. Before calling its contents boring, notice how much depends on what else the household can manage.
Adult brings small basket into original modest room; table and hearth unchanged.

chapters.title: A small dinner is not the same as no food culture
scenes: Bread belongs at the centre of this table. Mercier calls it a principal food of the poor in large French towns.
Substantial round loaf with cut slice on plain board; imperfect crust, no baguette.
Beside our loaf sits the small sausage portion. We will not make the diners into a joke.
Two adults prepare simple bread and sausage, normal healthy proportions, calm expressions.
They are choosing within limits. Our Visitor has come to understand, rather than write a restaurant review.
Visitor observes clear table left, no rude disgust expression or phone.
The amount of meat is modest here. But the claim that ordinary Parisians never ate meat fails against Mercier's own descriptions.
Small portion shown honestly next to bread, no empty plate implying universal starvation.
He names soup and boiled beef at dinner, with other beef preparations in the evening.
Three period-food icons: bowl of soup, modest boiled beef, covered pot; no exact portion sizes.
He also mentions Sunday mutton. That describes a meal pattern, not everyone's ability to afford it.
Covered meat basket and modest mutton portion on stall, no Sunday festival crowd.
Poverty has degrees. A household scraping together a small purchase is not interchangeable with a comfortable family employing a servant.
Small room and limited hearth seen together; people treated with dignity.
Our single table is a comparison, not an unchanging national menu.
Same meal viewed from different side; no calendar or repeated identical plates.
The room for adjustment is narrow. Another dish requires another ingredient from somewhere.
Small basket now empty beside table, Visitor right considering it.
And having food in the room is not the final step. Cooking needs a place, heat, utensils and somebody doing the work.
Small hearth with plain pot and a few pieces of firewood, adult attending safely.
Keep that hearth in mind. Later, another Parisian household will solve a cooking problem by carrying its dinner out of the house.
Commercial masonry oven and two covered household dishes on bench, no customers yet.
The bread is cut and the small dish shared. Modest food can matter greatly to its diners.
Two adults sit with proportionate slices and small sausage pieces; no Visitor awkward seating.
The rich table looks more generous. Follow it behind the scenes, where somebody prepares the food.
Comfortable dining room with doorway toward kitchen/service route; table modestly populated.
Follow the Visitor through that door. A surprisingly ordinary vegetable is about to acquire a very elaborate supporting cast.
Kitchen worktop with cabbage, modest ham and mushrooms, cook at hearth left; clear right for Visitor.

chapters.title: What wealth adds to the plate
scenes: Our affluent dinner includes roast poultry. Both Mercier's shops and Menon's earlier cookbook put poultry comfortably within this culinary world.
Golden roast poultry on ordinary elegant platter, white cloth, two side dishes, no giant banquet.
The book appeared in seventeen fifty-five. We choose one period recipe for our imagined seventeen-eighty-three household.
Prepared bird on worktable near spit, source label local, no named family crest.
Menon • Les Soupers de la Cour,1755
Its roast section discusses preparing poultry and serving it with the right colour. The finished platter is the endpoint of skilled handling.
Cook checks spit-roasted bird visually, hearth controlled; avoid depicting outdated food-storage advice.
At our imagined table, there are several dishes to choose among. The diners have room for preferences beyond making one purchase last.
Two diners, poultry platter, cabbage garnish, bread and sauce bowl; exactly four food groups.
Mercier mocks affluent diners demanding novelty even when surrounded by elaborate food.
Keep actual selected food arrangement legible; no exotic turtle, pineapple tower or lobster pile.
His spoiled diner is a satirical figure. Our composite table does not turn that caricature into every wealthy person.
Diners ordinary and composed, no greedy villain expressions.
A simpler contrast is visible right here: a person serving, dishes arriving, and diners who can remain at the table.
Servant sets a cabbage dish at left, diners seated; clear ground for Visitor right.
In this composite household, somebody else's work keeps dinner moving. That work does not appear as a separate ingredient on the plate.
Servant carries modest platter along short service route, no impossible floating tray.
The cabbage is an unlikely luxury. A plain vegetable announces less than a decorated room.
One cabbage quarter close-up, clean worktop, no silver or jewels.
Now open Menon's recipe. It turns that cabbage into a garnish around meat, with several stages before it reaches the table.
Quartered cabbage beside plain cooking pot, no invented recipe lettering.
Its sauce adds ingredients and operations. The vegetable's name gives you only part of the dinner.
Ham slice, mushrooms, garlic clove, small stock bowl and pan arranged clearly; no cream or butter added.
So the wealthy version of an ordinary ingredient may carry a kitchen's time and resources inside something that looks deceptively simple.
Cooked cabbage garnish around meat with restrained brown sauce, no raw cabbage on finished plate.
You cannot read all that work just by looking at the dish. We need to rewind from the table to the pan.
Worktop and hearth, cook at left, clean space for a locally added KITCHEN caption.
This reveals more than simply comparing which household has the larger piece of meat.
Cabbage, pan and plain bowl, simple composition preparing next process scene.

chapters.title: Follow the cabbage
scenes: Menon's seventeen-fifty-five recipe begins by blanching the cut cabbage. This is our period example, not a recovered family's menu.
Cabbage pieces in plain pot of hot water, no numerical temperature; source label local.
The cabbage is cooled and squeezed before further cooking. Several actions hide behind one word on a menu.
Cook's normal hands gently squeeze cooled cabbage above plain bowl; no Visitor hand or boiling handling.
Next comes braising. The recipe gives the vegetable its own preparation before placing it around the meat.
Covered plain braising pot beside cabbage bowl, no modern stovetop or invented duration.
Even the arrangement has a purpose: the cabbage becomes a garnish around another dish, rather than the whole meal.
Cabbage arranged around meat on platter, food proportions modest; no raw ingredients on dining table.
But we have not finished. A separate sauce brings in ham, mushrooms, and garlic studded with a clove.
Exactly ham slice, mushrooms and garlic with one clove beside pan, ingredient forms readable.
These ingredients do work in the recipe. They are not decorations beside the pan.
Same ingredients beginning in small pan at hearth edge; no stove knobs or modern utensils.
The recipe then adds broth and coulis. The pan is carrying more than the cabbage's own flavour.
Small earthen jug pouring brown broth into pan, one clear normal hand; no cream.
Period savoury coulis • not a modern fruit sauce
It is reduced to a sauce and strained. A plain-looking vegetable has brought another pan and a sieve into the story.
Sauce poured through plain sieve over bowl; gravity and connected pouring stream correct.
Pepper finishes this part of the preparation. We have crossed several stages without needing a fantastically rare centrepiece.
Finished brown sauce in simple bowl, coarse pepper nearby, no huge spice heap.
Extra ingredients, equipment and heat give this cook more options than the other table's small purchase.
Four icons: ingredients, pan, fire, hands; no numerical cost comparison.
The finished plate conceals much of that process. You see cabbage; the kitchen has handled a chain of preparations.
Finished cabbage garnish and poultry on restrained platter; sauce coating light enough to see shapes.
Our Visitor distrusts the word 'simple.' It can describe a result while ignoring the effort.
Cabbage dish clear left, Visitor considers it at right.
We have demonstrated one cookbook's recipe, without ordering it for every wealthy Parisian.
Cook and chosen ingredients at same worktop, no row of identical households.
Now change the problem. Suppose you have bought meat, but your home offers little more than a hearth.
Right-side hearth and covered purchased meat dish on board table; separate household, olive plaster and left square window.

chapters.title: Dinner goes out to be cooked
scenes: Mercier describes small households sending meat to pastry-shop ovens. Buying the food did not mean owning the best place to cook it.
Adult customer delivers covered earthenware dish to baker, plain oven behind.
This household can afford the meat. It need not be as poor as our first composite.
Modestly dressed customer and baker at counter, no wealth indicators or starvation exaggeration.
Their solution is practical: carry the dish to somebody whose oven is already part of a working business.
Covered household dish on bench beside oven peel; no name or numbered ticket.
The household pays for cooking and saves on wood at home. Fuel belongs in the cost of dinner too.
Masonry oven, small stack of wood, baker attending; no price sign.
This arrangement links the home kitchen to a commercial one. Our imagined dinner has left the house without becoming a restaurant outing.
Same pastry shop with household customer departing, no restaurant seating or modern waiter uniform.
Mercier grumbles about quality and handling. Paying someone else did not guarantee a perfect roast.
Cooked household dish on bench, modest browned roast, no deliberately charred disaster or filthy handler.
But the service itself is revealing. Space and fuel can matter alongside the ingredients in deciding how a household eats.
Same second modest home with right hearth, covered dish absent on its shop-oven journey, no large oven.
If you only compare two finished plates, that journey to the oven disappears. Follow the dish, and another part of the city appears.
Shop doorway and carried dish at left, Visitor right watching.
Our wealthy household brings work behind its dining-room door. Another household carries food to where the heat is.
Affluent household kitchen with hearth and worktable, restrained staff count, no workers standing idle.
These are different ways of arranging labour and equipment. A meal has a history before anybody sits down to eat it.
Two routes: home kitchen to table; household dish to shop oven and back. Arrows never imply all poor families use same route.
TWO ROUTES TO A COOKED MEAL
And its history may continue afterwards. At the richer table, we have been following the diners. Now watch the person clearing away.
Servant lifts partly served poultry platter, normal hands and stable crockery.
The food leaving the room is not necessarily finished with. There is a third place at this comparison that we have barely considered.
Plain side table beyond dining doorway, partially served platter and bread, no servant eating yet.

chapters.title: The third place at the table
scenes: Mercier makes a pointed observation: servants in wealthy households could eat better than some people living in modest bourgeois homes.
Ordinary servant sits by side table with modest portion from remaining food, no opulent feast or stolen property.
Mercier’s social observation • not every servant
His comparison is about access to food, not a claim that serving somebody gave you control over their money or household.
Servant's plain bowl and bread beside larger cleared platter; visual difference between portion and ownership.
The contrast complicates our two tables. The person carrying a dish may have a relationship to its contents beyond simply transporting it.
Serving platter left, ordinary servant background, Visitor attentive right.
This is Mercier's observation, not a generous leftover allowance guaranteed to every servant.
Partly served poultry platter on plain table, no exact portions assigned to all workers.
There is another route for food after dinner. Menon's cookbook explicitly begins one recipe with leftover roast poultry.
Small bowl of chopped cooked poultry from earlier roast beside thin pastry, no fresh raw bird.
That poultry becomes a filling, enclosed between thin pieces of pastry. The finished rissoles are shaped as little crescents.
One open pastry round with filling and two correctly sealed crescents, simple worktop.
They are fried to a golden colour. Poultry from an earlier meal can return to the table in another form.
Golden crescent rissoles on simple plate beside plain pan; no claim of exact overnight storage.
The recipe demonstrates reuse. It cannot tell us what happened to every plate in Paris.
Finished pastry plate and remaining poultry bowl together; no universal recycling diagram.
So our rich-and-poor comparison has acquired cooks, shop ovens, servants and a second use for food that looked finished.
Four connected but distinct icons, no claim they all served one documented household.
We have moved beyond a feast facing an empty plate.
Return to substantial loaf and small sausage dish with actual food, no poverty caricature.
Inequality remains, expressed through more than two dinners at first glance.
Comfortable dining room after meal, selected dishes partly empty, no food mountain or discarded leftovers.
Our Visitor admires the cooking while noticing who supplies the time and who must stretch a purchase.
Cook at work left, Visitor respectful right; quiet composition.

chapters.title: What the two dinners reveal
scenes: Back at the modest table, the meal is shared. Back at the richer one, people have had more room to choose.
Two adults with simple food, relaxed dignity, no bleak tears or comic eating.
The difference includes how much arrives, but also who prepares it, where it cooks, and what happens to the remains.
Dining doorway frames service table beyond; keep same architecture and no duplicated platter.
A small piece of sausage disproved one easy stereotype. A cabbage showed how much effort can hide inside an ordinary ingredient.
Sausage/bread and cabbage/sauce icons side by side, with no claim identical nutritive value.
The shared oven added fuel and space. The service table showed why a person's position alone does not describe every mouthful.
Plain servant portion near cleared platter, doorway to rich room visible.
These dinners do not explain the entire Revolution. They help us see unequal lives in the same city before it.
Paris market in late afternoon, ordinary buyers, no revolution flags or guillotine.
